> # Plan: Three-Turn Seed Runway + Less Law-Dominated Writing
>
> ## Summary
>
> Change seeding from “one opening choice node” to a small playable runway: an intro turn with a cosmetic choice, a second turn with real choices, and third-turn branch nodes already authored inside the seed packet. At the same time, rebalance Writer instructions so the binding doctrine supports story conflict instead of taking over the whole premise.
>
> ## Key Changes
>
> - **Seed packet shape**
>   - Keep the existing 5-node packet cap.
>   - Seed packets must use this structure:
>     - `turn_1_intro`: fake onboarding choice node; 2-3 flavor choices all target the same next node and do not affect state.
>     - `turn_2_decision`: normal playable node with exactly 3 real choices.
>     - `turn_3_branch_a/b/c`: one prebuilt branch node per real choice.
>   - Turn-3 branch nodes are terminal handoff nodes with `revision_notes` for Writer continuation after they are narrated.
>
> - **Play loop behavior**
>   - If a selected choice has a valid `target_node_id` in the current packet, follow that target before calling Writer refresh.
>   - Writer refresh remains default for free text, missing targets, terminal handoff continuation, or after the prebuilt runway is exhausted.
>   - Persist each narrated runway turn as normal story reading material.
>
> - **Writer seed instructions**
>   - Replace “opening aim: one taboo/law” with “opening aim: player, desire, place, pressure, opposition, and a choice that reveals character.”
>   - Demote binding doctrine to one StoryBible support element, not the organizing center of every workshop turn.
>   - Rewrite workshop turns around story engine:
>     - imagination: varied premises with player desire and first irreversible pressure;
>     - selection: compare finalists by player hook, antagonist/opposition, novelty, and playable choice;
>     - engine: develop conflict, cast pressure, material world, and doctrine only where it sharpens conflict;
>     - runway: design the 3-turn playable sequence.
>
> - **Verifier/taste gate**
>   - Reject valid seeds where law/doctrine is the dominant dramatic subject.
>   - Reject seeds whose first turn is mostly system explanation, civic procedure, or invented terminology.
>   - Require visible player desire, active opposition, and choices that express stance rather than only navigation.
>   - Require the fake intro choice to be explicitly non-branching and the second-turn choices to target the three third-turn nodes.
>
> - **Scenarist/tool use**
>   - Workshop Writer can call scenarists and lore expert.
>   - Final constrained bundle Writer does not get `call_scenarists` by default; it reads workshop artifacts and packages the seed.
>   - Scenarists are prompted to brainstorm story heat, player conflict, reversals, and reader criticism before doctrine mechanics.
>
> ## Test Plan
>
> - Unit tests:
>   - seed prompt requires the 5-node runway shape;
>   - seed verifier rejects missing fake-choice node, more/less than 3 real choices, and missing third-turn branch nodes;
>   - play loop follows valid in-packet targets before Writer refresh;
>   - final seed Writer runner excludes `call_scenarists`;
>   - verifier rejects law-dominated valid bundles.
>
> - CLI tests:
>   - static seed produces intro -> real choice -> selected branch over three turns without Writer refresh;
>   - after the third runway turn, Writer refresh is invoked for continuation;
>   - `go test ./...` remains green.
>
> - Manual smoke:
>   - `go run ./cmd/cli`;
>   - first turn should feel like story onboarding, not the main dilemma;
>   - second turn presents three meaningful choices;
>   - third turn follows the selected branch before any Writer refresh.
>
> ## Assumptions
>
> - Opening seed uses exactly 3 real choices to preserve the current 5-node cap.
> - Fake intro choices are cosmetic onboarding, not canon-changing decisions.
> - Binding doctrine remains required in the StoryBible, but it should serve character conflict rather than dominate the prose.
</details>

One structural wrinkle: the current packet validator caps packets at 5 nodes. Your 3-turn seed shape is `intro node + real choice node + one branch node per real choice`, so 4 real choices would require 6 nodes. That is solvable, but it’s a product decision: either seed real choices cap at 3, or raise seed packet cap to 6 for this opening packet.

The prompt is fighting the Writer.

Main issue: the “Imagination Turn” says *free-form creative workshop*, but then injects final-bundle obligations, packet topology, validation rules, canon boundaries, tool policy, and doctrine language. So the model’s creative attention gets pulled toward compliance instead of story heat.

**Remove**
- Remove final bundle/packet details from free-form workshop turns:
  - “Return a durable StoryBible…”
  - “The seed packet is a three-turn runway…”
  - all `turn_1_intro`, `turn_2_decision`, target-node rules.
- Remove repeated “Do not…” blocks where one positive boundary is enough.
- Remove “binding doctrine” from the Imagination Turn except as one optional ingredient.
- Remove “Metabarons canon…” specificity from the main creative prompt body; keep only the DNA summary.

**Reword**
- “Protect reader plausibility” -> “Make the strange feel lived-in: give it a cause, a daily use, a human cost, and a visible consequence.”
- “Treat doctrine as support…” -> “A local rule may sharpen conflict, but the story should start from a person wanting something under pressure.”
- “Use material imagination…” -> “Start from concrete matter: work, weather, disease, hunger, craft, architecture, tools, scars, rituals, machines, language.”

**Add**
- Put the actual creative task first, before tool instructions.
- Ask for more human story ingredients: protagonist want, wound, opponent, relationship pressure, image, irreversible trouble.
- Tell the Writer what “good” feels like:
  - playable
  - emotionally legible
  - surprising
  - concrete
  - not a civic-procedure explainer
- For tool use, make it short: Scenarists are for idea sparks and critique; LoreExpert is for source-pattern questions.

I’d reshape the Imagination prompt like this:

```text
You are the Creative Writer for a Sans-Nom seed workshop.

This turn is for invention only. Think like a comics storyteller looking for the hot center of a playable science-fantasy story.

Create 6-8 original story germs. For each germ, include:
- a vivid first image
- who the player character is
- what they want right now
- who or what actively opposes them
- the wound, guilt, hunger, or loyalty that makes the choice personal
- the strange material condition of the world
- the first irreversible pressure point
- why this could become a playable opening

Favor concrete story heat over explanation. Start from bodies, tools, work, weather, disease, hunger, craft, architecture, rituals, machines, language, scars, inheritance, or relationships.

Make the strange feel lived-in: give it a cause, a daily use, a human cost, and a visible consequence.

The selected lore pack is influence DNA only: operatic science-fantasy comics, body and taboo pressure, witness memory, family/function/refusal tension, spectacle, and philosophical consequence. Transform the influence into new names, new places, new conflicts, and new social orders.

A local rule or doctrine may appear if it sharpens character conflict, but the story should begin with a person wanting something under pressure.

Use call_scenarists when you want outside sparks, critique, alternative premises, character contradictions, scene engines, or reader-risk checks. Use ask_lore_expert only for focused source-pattern research.

Output Markdown only. Do not produce the final structured seed.
```

Then keep the three-turn runway rules only in the final constrained bundle prompt. The workshop should make raw ore; the final turn can make rails.

> lets reduce the also the number of original story germs, it feels too much

Yes. I’d reduce it to **3-4 germs**, not 5-8 or 6-8.

The current count pushes the Writer into list-making mode. For creative quality, we want fewer candidates with more texture: one strange image, one protagonist want, one opposition, one wound, one irreversible pressure.

Recommended wording:

```text
Create 3-4 original story germs. Make each one distinct enough to compete as the seed for the whole story.
```

And add:

```text
Prefer depth over coverage. A strong germ should feel playable, emotionally specific, and visually memorable after one paragraph.
```

So the Imagination Turn becomes less “generate options” and more “discover a few live wires.”

>
> ## Summary
> Refactor all story-generation prompts so creative turns produce stronger story material instead of compliance-shaped lists. The core rule: each prompt should lead with the role’s actual creative job, keep constraints local to the phase, prefer positive guidance over repeated prohibitions, and move schema/legal packet rules out of free-form workshop turns.
>
> ## Key Changes
> - **Shared prompt philosophy**
>   - Use fewer, deeper creative outputs: Imagination Turn generates `3-4` story germs, not `5-8`.
>   - Put story heat first: player desire, active opposition, wound, relationship pressure, vivid image, irreversible trouble.
>   - Replace abstract compliance phrasing with creative criteria: playable, emotionally specific, visually memorable, strange-but-lived-in.
>   - Keep “do not” rules sparse and only for hard boundaries: no canon copying, no JSON/schema in free-form turns, no missing packet targets in structured turns.
>
> - **Seed workshop prompts**
>   - Remove final `StoryBible`, `StoryPacket`, runway-node, and target-node rules from free-form workshop turns.
>   - Reframe workshop turns around creative process:
>     - Imagination: `3-4` rich germs, depth over coverage.
>     - Selection: compare finalists by player hook, opposition, freshness, emotional clarity, and playable pressure.
>     - Engine: develop protagonist, opponent, cast friction, material world, reversals, and local doctrine only where it sharpens conflict.
>     - Runway: design the three-turn playable opening in prose/planning terms, still without schema fields.
>   - Keep tool guidance short: Scenarists for sparks/critique; LoreExpert for focused source-pattern research.
>
> - **Final seed bundle prompt**
>   - Move all strict runway and schema requirements here:
>     - exactly 5 nodes;
>     - intro fake-choice node;
>     - second-turn decision with exactly 3 real choices;
>     - three terminal third-turn branch nodes;
>     - every target resolves inside the packet.
>   - State that workshop material is advisory raw ore; the final Writer owns selection, compression, and structure.
>   - Preserve strict validation, but make the prompt story-first before packet-contract details.
>
> - **Writer refresh, Scenarist, LoreExpert, Narrator**
>   - Writer refresh should focus on continuing from current canon, player decision, immediate consequence, and next playable pressure; packet closure rules stay present but compact.
>   - Scenarist prompts should ask for brainstorming, criticism, alternatives, risks, images, reversals, and scene engines; avoid asking them to choose a final story unless the Writer will read that answer before a dependent next call.
>   - LoreExpert prompts stay influence-only and source-pattern-focused; they should not become a creative substitute for Scenarists.
>   - Narrator prompts should emphasize scene, character action, sensory specificity, and emotional movement; doctrine/law should appear through lived consequence instead of exposition.
>
> - **Verifier/taste gates**
>   - Keep hard structural validation unchanged.
>   - Add/keep qualitative rejection for seeds that are mostly procedure, terminology, doctrine exposition, or world-system explanation.
>   - Require first turns to foreground player, desire, place, pressure, opposition, and a character-revealing choice.
>
> ## Test Plan
> - Unit-test prompt text:
>   - free-form workshop prompts no longer contain `StoryBible`, `StoryPacket`, runway node IDs, or target-node closure rules;
>   - Imagination prompt asks for `3-4` germs and “depth over coverage”;
>   - final seed prompt contains the full 5-node runway contract;
>   - Writer refresh keeps compact closure rules;
>   - Scenarist and LoreExpert prompts describe their distinct roles.
> - Regression-test behavior:
>   - static seed still produces a valid 5-node runway;
>   - free-form workshop artifacts are not indexed as canon or committed;
>   - final seed validation still rejects malformed packets and law/doctrine-dominated openings.
> - Run:
>   - `go test ./...`
>   - admin prompt-log inspection on a live seed to confirm the workshop prompt is shorter, less schema-heavy, and more creative-facing.
>
> ## Assumptions
> - The seed workshop should maximize creative material, not structural compliance.
> - Strict packet shape belongs only in final constrained bundle generation and validation.
> - Scenarists remain idea/critique assistants; the Creative Writer remains responsible for final story authorship.
</details>

> # Sequential Scenarist Sessions
>
> ## Summary
> The stopped run confirms this is not a wording problem. The Writer used the tool exactly as the API invited it to: three parallel Scenarists, three disconnected idea streams, plus direct lore-file reads. Fix the tool shape and runtime: Scenarist work becomes one synchronous advisory session at a time, while LoreExpert remains the only source-lore specialist.
>
> ## Key Changes
> - Replace `call_scenarists` with a single-request `ask_scenarist` tool.
>   - Tool input is one `topic_id`, `topic`, `request`, `hard_boundaries`, and `relevant_paths`, not a `requests[]` batch.
>   - One call writes one Markdown artifact and returns one path.
>   - Multiple Scenarist passes require multiple tool calls, so the Writer can read prior answers before asking follow-up questions.
>   - Remove parallel goroutines from `ToolRunner.Handle`; provider pools become round-robin/fallback selection, not simultaneous creative synthesis.
>
> - Remove prompt-level parallelism guidance entirely.
>   - Writer prompts say: ask one Scenarist for one clear advisory job, read the answer, then ask a follow-up only if needed.
>   - Scenarist prompts say: answer the current request from provided context and relevant paths; if dependent material is missing, state what path/input is needed.
>   - Final seed bundle generation still has no Scenarist tool; it reads workshop artifacts and authors the structured seed itself.
>
> - Stop Scenarists from bypassing LoreExpert for source lore.
>   - Remove direct `lore/packs/...` read pointers and the `lore` add-dir from Scenarist tool sessions.
>   - Scenarists may read only workshop/story artifact paths explicitly passed through `relevant_paths`.
>   - Source-pattern grounding goes through `@LoreExpert`, which stays cached, influence-only, and logged.
>
> - Clean up configuration around the new behavior.
>   - Replace `-writer-scenarists` with `-writer-scenarist-calls`; default live value enables sequential calls, `0` disables.
>   - Keep actual provider/model metadata on each Scenarist artifact and backstage bubble.
>   - Rename logs from `scenarist.call.*` to `scenarist.ask.*`, with one material per event.
>
> ## Test Plan
> - Unit tests:
>   - `ask_scenarist` schema accepts exactly one request and has no `requests[]`.
>   - ToolRunner writes one artifact per call and never runs provider calls concurrently.
>   - Provider pool rotates providers across sequential calls.
>   - Writer workshop prompts contain no “parallel” wording.
>   - Scenarist system prompt exposes no direct lore-pack file pointers.
>   - Scenarist source-pattern questions route through LoreExpert.
>
> - Regression tests:
>   - A model attempting the old batched `call_scenarists` shape cannot run because that tool is unavailable.
>   - A dependent follow-up works by reading the first returned artifact path and passing it as `relevant_paths` in the next `ask_scenarist`.
>   - Backstage shows ordered `@Scenarist` request/response pairs instead of same-timestamp parallel answer clusters.
>   - Logs show no Scenarist `Read` calls under `lore/packs/...`.
>
> - Verification:
>   - `go test ./...`
>   - Manual seed smoke: start a live seed, stop after the first workshop turn, verify Scenarist calls appear sequential and each later request can reference earlier artifact paths.
>
> ## Assumptions
> - We prefer a structural fix over more prompt tuning.
> - Losing parallel speed is acceptable because coherent seed material matters more than three fast disconnected drafts.
> - Scenarists remain creative brainstormers/critics; LoreExpert remains the source-lore research path.
</details>

> ## I. The Witness-Tongue's Silence
>
> **Opening Image:** A woman with silver-thread scars tracing her throat like a map of witnesses stands before the Tribunal of Keeps. Her daughter kneels hooded in the drowning-pool, water already at her chin. The mother has seen the crime that never happened.
>
> **Strange Material Condition:** In this world, memory is written into tissue. Witness-Tongues carry bio-lattice modifications that record precisely what their eyes take in. They can speak truthfully about any witnessed death—and they *must* speak if called before a Tribunal. But silence is their right. To lie about a witnessed death is death. To speak when silence is owed is the same. The scars map the body as deaths accumulate, branching, climbing, until a veteran witness-Tongue is more scar than skin.
>
> **Protagonist Desire:** Save her daughter from execution by revealing the truth of what she witnessed—the crime the Tribunal claims never occurred.
>
> **Active Opposition:** The Keepers enforce the Silence-Oath that binds all Witness-Tongues. If she speaks what she saw, she breaks the oath and becomes an oathbreaker: executed by the same drowning ritual, her testimony erased, her scars burned away so her witnessed memories die with her. Her daughter lives in her silence. Her daughter dies in her speech.
>
> **Emotional Wound:** Guilt of failure. Seven years ago, she watched her husband's murder and kept silent—to protect her daughter from being next. Her daughter has grown up believing her father simply vanished. The daughter does not know her mother chose her life over truth.
>
> **Relationship Pressure:** The daughter has discovered her mother witnessed something. If the mother speaks, the daughter learns the truth of her father's murder—and also learns her mother watched and said nothing. The daughter's love curdles into accusation. If the mother stays silent, the daughter dies not knowing, and the mother carries that ignorance as her final gift to her child.
>
> **Irreversible First Pressure:** The daughter, hooded and drowning, opens her mouth underwater. The mother has three breaths to choose: speak the truth and watch her own execution ordered, or remain silent and watch her daughter sink. There is no middle path. The water is already rising.
>
> ---
>
> ## II. The Bone-Singer's Last Frequency
>
> **Opening Image:** A woman whose spine has begun to grow hollow organ-pipes of bone stands before the Ash Lords' chamber. Her breath carries the faint hum of harmonics that shouldn't exist outside a reactor-temple. She is the last craftsperson who can sing the stabilizing frequency. Without her, the temple burns.
>
> **Strange Material Condition:** The Singing Guild teaches bone-resonance: through decades of practice, a craftsperson's skeleton literally reshapes to match the frequencies they master. Their bones become instruments. But the final transformation—that which allows true harmonic control—requires the Bone-Singer to absorb resonance directly from reactor-temples, which slowly replaces their marrow with crystallized harmonic energy. They become architecture. They become infrastructure. They become necessary.
>
> **Protagonist Desire:** Remain human enough to leave the temple and find her missing apprentice before the Ash Lords use her as permanent power supply.
>
> **Active Opposition:** The Ash Lords' Accord demands that any fully-transformed Bone-Singer surrender their throat to the temple's service. They have already sent Silence-Keepers to seal her vocal cords if she refuses. They do not care if she dies; they care only that the frequency persists.
>
> **Emotional Wound:** She remembers when singing was craft, not consumption. She let her mentor be taken for transformation because she was too afraid to speak against the Accord. She watched him become the temple's heart and told herself it was honorable. She was wrong. She has carried that cowardice for twenty years.

Implemented the scene-session fix and actor-boundary cleanup.

What changed:
- Honcho commits now use a scene-scoped session id derived from `base session + packet + node`, so each narrated scene gets its own Honcho room. This avoids observer accumulation and keeps actors from inheriting events from scenes they were not present for.
- Context assembly now queries the scene-scoped session, while still keeping the packet’s original `session_id` as the story-level seed so Writer packets do not compound scene IDs.
- Actor model calls now get a scene-local context, not the full narrator/story context.
- Unsupported `actor_needs` are pruned before narrator context assembly and before saved Writer packets.
- Narrator `surfaced_actor_messages` are only committed as actor-surface events when that actor actually had a real local actor output/card. Fake generated ids like `drip_notary_shell` no longer become Honcho actor peers.

- [cmd/cli/main.go](./cmd/cli/main.go)

The Writer was emitting `actor_needs` for story entities that have no actor cards, so the runtime kept skipping them. Now those needs are filtered and logged as filtered, not invoked/skipped repeatedly.

Found the smell and patched the main leak.

What was happening:
- `Bell` was embedded in the static seed in [internal/seed/seed.go](./internal/seed/seed.go:563). I removed those static “ninth bell” references.
- More importantly, the workshop manifest used `previewText(output, 600)`, so if the first generated germ was “Bell-Hunger”, that raw motif got copied into every later workshop prompt. That is exactly the kind of self-reinforcing context pollution we were worried about.

> What I found: there are two different leaks.
>
> 1. Codex Writer/Narrator read tools are rooted at the real repo root, so `rg`, `find`, `cat`, etc. can see code, tests, fixtures, old seed runs, logs, and every story.
> 2. Claude-style Scenarists have a narrower `WorkDir/AddDirs`, but the prompt still tells them the repo root path, which tempts them to reach outside the intended material.
>
> The clean design choice is whether we want to solve this by creating a curated “agent workspace” per run, or by adding stricter path allowlists around the current repo. I have a strong preference, but this is a product/ops tradeoff worth locking.
>
> Plan
>
> # Agent-Scoped Filesystem Plan
>
> ## Summary
> Replace repo-root tool access with per-run curated agent workspaces. Writer, Narrator, and Scenarist file tools will see only active story/seed material made for that run. Direct source-lore filesystem access is reserved for LoreExpert; creative agents use `ask_lore_expert` for source-pattern grounding.
>
> ## Key Changes
> - Add an `agentfs` workspace layer that creates scoped roots under the active run:
>   - Seed runs: `data/seed-runs/<seed_id>/agent/`
>   - Story runs: `data/stories/<story_id>/agent/<role>/<run_id-or-turn>/`
>   - Include only curated files: current state summary, bible, current packet/node, narration needed for continuity, current workshop/scenarist artifacts, and model-run diagnostics relevant to that role.
> - Stop rooting local tools at the repository root:
>   - Writer refresh, seed workshop Writer, final seed Writer, and Narrator use `ToolRoot = agentfs.Root`.
>   - Claude-style Scenarists use `WorkDir/AddDirs = agentfs.Root` only.
>   - Remove “Repository root:” from Scenarist prompts; replace with “Workspace root:” when tools are enabled.
> - Keep LoreExpert as the only direct source-lore specialist:
>   - Creative agents do not receive `lore/packs/...` paths.
>   - `ask_lore_expert` remains cached and influence-only; it may use the active lore-pack internally.
>   - Any `relevant_paths` passed to `ask_scenarist` must resolve inside the current agent workspace.
> - Normalize returned artifact paths:
>   - `ask_scenarist` writes artifacts into the scoped agent workspace and returns workspace-relative paths the Writer can read immediately.
>   - Durable logs/admin still record the real artifact path, but model-visible paths stay scoped.
> - Harden tool execution:
>   - Reject absolute paths outside the scoped root, `..` escapes, and attempts to read repo surfaces like `cmd/`, `internal/`, `testdata/`, `.git/`, unrelated `data/stories`, or old `data/seed-runs`.
>   - Add log fields for `agent_workspace_root`, `visible_paths`, and rejected path attempts.
>
> ## Interface Changes
> - Add a small `agentfs.Scope` type with:
>   - `Root`
>   - `Role`
>   - `StoryID` / `SeedRunID`
>   - `VisiblePaths`
>   - helpers to stage/copy allowed files and resolve returned paths.
> - Extend runner setup to accept an `agentfs.Scope` instead of raw `materialDir`/repo-root decisions.
> - Update `scenarist.ToolRunner` to validate `relevant_paths` against the scope and return scoped artifact paths.
>
> ## Test Plan
> - Unit tests:
>   - Writer/Narrator Codex runners never set `ToolRoot` to `repoRoot()`.
>   - Scenarist prompts no longer include repo root and only expose workspace-root wording.
>   - `ask_scenarist` rejects `lore/packs/...`, `cmd/...`, `internal/...`, `testdata/...`, absolute repo paths, and old story/seed paths.
>   - `ask_scenarist` returns a path readable from the Writer’s scoped tool root.
>   - LoreExpert remains the only component allowed to inspect active lore-pack source material.
> - Regression tests:
>   - Seed workshop still runs all turns and final bundle can read workshop/scenarist artifacts.
>   - Writer refresh can read its own diagnostics and current story artifacts, but not unrelated stories.
>   - Narrator read tools can inspect current turn/story material only.
>   - Admin/backstage artifact links still resolve to durable files.
> - Run:
>   - `go test -count=1 ./...`
>
> ## Assumptions
> - Direct active lore-pack filesystem access is not exposed to Writer, Narrator, or Scenarist in v1.
> - Existing story/seed data remains readable by the app; only future model-visible tool roots change.
> - Generated agent workspaces are runtime artifacts and are not committed.
</details>

What changed:

- Seed runs now place model-visible workshop/scenarist material under `data/seed-runs/<seed>/agent/`.
- Story Writer/Narrator runs now get scoped roots under `data/stories/<story_id>/agent/<role>/<run>/`.
- Writer/Narrator Codex tools no longer use `repoRoot()` as `ToolRoot`.
- Scenarist prompts now say `Workspace root`, not repo root.
- `ask_scenarist` validates `relevant_paths` against the scoped workspace and rejects repo/code/lore/old story paths.
- Local `exec_command` now rejects absolute paths and repo-surface paths outside the agent workspace, not just escaped `workdir`.
- Scenarist/workshop artifacts return model-readable workspace-relative paths, while logs/admin keep durable artifact paths.

Fixed. The failure was real: `ask_scenarist` still leaked the durable path back to the Writer in some cases, especially when the seed agent root was relative. The Writer then tried to read `data/seed-runs/.../agent/...`, and the scoped tool guard correctly rejected it.

I changed it so:
- agent scope roots are absolute internally;
- seed scenarist output dirs are absolute internally;
- model-visible Scenarist paths stay workspace-relative like `scenarists/tool-call-001/01-imagination-germs.md`;
- `artifact_path` is kept for logs/admin, but no longer returned to the model/tool response;
- admin backstage can still resolve the durable artifact path from log detail.

Added a regression for exactly this case: relative durable output dir, but `ask_scenarist` response exposes only `scenarists/...`.

> A young diver named **Iren Voss** kneels on the keel of a sunken cathedral-ship while silver fish chew the last wedding veil from her hair. Above her, the floating city of **Nacre-Hook** drifts on chains through a white corrosive sea; below her, inside the drowned nave, her dead husband’s reflection is still alive in a salt mirror big as a door. Iren wants one thing before the tide turns: to break the mirror and free his trapped image before his powerful family uses it to annul their marriage, erase her claim, and take back the child growing in her body.
>
> In Nacre-Hook, marriage is not sealed by vow but by **reflection exchange**. Lovers stand before a polished salt slab, and each reflection is cut loose and stored as proof of union. If one spouse dies, the surviving reflection can be questioned, inherited, sold, or punished. A person without a reflection cannot own property, testify, or be buried in city stone. Iren’s wound is that she survived the wreck that killed her husband because she cut herself free from his diving harness; his family calls it cowardice, and some part of her believes them. His reflection remembers the drowning from an angle she cannot bear.
>
> Opposing her is **House Cormea**, pearl-armored salvagers who arrive with hooks, priest-lawyers, and a black pump that can drain a wreck without asking the sea’s permission. Her husband’s older sister, **Mava**, loved him viciously and blames Iren for stealing him from the family trade. Mava does not merely want the mirror; she wants Iren to hear the dead man condemn her in public. The relationship pressure sharpens because the reflection in the salt mirror still speaks tenderly to Iren, still calls her “my tide,” and may be either her husband’s preserved soul or only the legal echo of him trained to comfort whoever owns the slab.
>
> The first irreversible trouble comes when Iren cracks the salt mirror with a diver’s chisel. Instead of freeing him, she releases every reflection trapped in the drowned cathedral: generations of dead spouses pour upward through the water like pale skins, and each one remembers a different crime committed in the city above. The sea around the wreck turns black with witness. House Cormea sees it. The city’s chain bells begin to ring. Iren can still flee with one shard that contains her husband’s face, but if she does, Nacre-Hook will declare her unborn child property of the house until the reflection can be “recovered.” The first playable choice is intimate and dirty: save the shard, save herself, or surface with the truth and become the most hunted widow in the sea.
>
> ---
>
> ## The Orchard That Breathes for the Rich
>
> At dawn in **Vellum Reach**, workers climb ladders into trees with lungs instead of leaves. The fruit are soft blue sacs that inflate and deflate in the mist, each one containing an hour of clean breath for the nobles who live above the smog line. **Tav Ren**, a contract pruner with scarred lips and a stolen key under his tongue, has come to cut one forbidden fruit: the breath his little sister sold when she was twelve, now ripening on a private branch behind bone-glass.
>
> The city below the ridge is slowly drowning in industrial pollen. Poor families lease pieces of their future respiration to the orchard guild; each breath-fruit grows from a childhood illness, a laugh, a held scream, a first swim, a fever dream. Rich buyers inhale them through jeweled masks and call it medicine. Tav wants to buy back his sister’s lung-right before her wedding, because the contract matures tonight: if the fruit is harvested by anyone else, she will lose the ability to breathe unassisted and spend her married life plugged into a municipal bellows.
>
> His active opposition is not an abstract system but **Mistress Orra Quain**, orchard matriarch, who trained Tav, fed him, and still wears his dead father’s pruning knife as a sign of “family debt.” Orra knows Tav’s hand better than he does; she can identify a cut by the angle of the wound on a branch. Tav’s wound is that he once reported his father for stealing breath-fruit to save Tav’s mother, believing the guild’s promise of mercy. The guild made the father into compost for the oldest tree. Tav has spent years pruning leaves grown from his father’s calcium.
>
> The relationship pressure comes from Tav’s sister **Lio**, who does not want rescue if it means Tav becomes a thief and corpse-fertilizer. She has chosen the wedding because her fiancé’s family owns a legal breathing pump; she is trading love, shame, and survival in one bargain. Tav sees sacrifice. Lio sees him trying to make her a child again. Their argument can happen ten meters up in a breathing tree while fruit pulse around them like sleeping animals.
>
> The first irreversible trouble arrives when Tav cuts the wrong stem on purpose. The fruit opens in his hands and exhales Lio’s stolen childhood breath into his face. For one perfect minute, he feels her memory of running through rain before the pollen years, laughing with whole lungs. Then the orchard recognizes an unauthorized inhaler. Every lung-tree around him begins coughing alarm spores, the noble district’s air pumps shut, and Orra releases the grafted wardens: men and women with orchard roots threaded through their ribs. Tav can still carry the emptied fruit as evidence that the guild sells children’s bodies, but now Lio is already short one hour of breath, and the city above is choking loudly enough to blame him.
>
> ---
>
> ## The Bell-Maker’s Son
>
> In the cliff city of **Harrow Spire**, every execution begins with music. Condemned people are lowered into a bronze furnace alive, and their final heartbeat is cast into a bell that rings whenever their crime is repeated. **Nesh Ardent**, apprentice bell-maker and son of the city’s most revered execution-smith, hears a new bell ring before it has been made. It beats from inside his own chest.
>
> Nesh wants to prevent tomorrow’s casting: his mother, long believed dead, has been dragged back from the ash provinces and sentenced as a traitor. The city claims she tried to silence a bell twenty years ago. His father refuses to speak of it except to say the family law: **a bell-maker does not question the metal once it screams**. Nesh has grown up proud of that doctrine, half craftsman and half priest, polishing bells made from murderers, oath-breakers, poisoners, deserters. Now the furnace wants his mother, and the craft he loves has become a mouth waiting to eat her.
>
> The strange material condition is civic and bodily. Harrow Spire’s laws are audible. Bells made from the dead hang in every market, nursery, bathhouse, court, and bedroom. Citizens learn morality by sound: a theft-bell twitches when a hand nears another purse; a lust-bell hums in certain alleys; a treason-bell tolls only when someone lies about the city’s founding. Nobody remembers law as text. They remember it as vibration in the bones. Deafness is considered a dangerous freedom. Children born deaf are given temple implants or sent below the cliff.
>
> Nesh’s wound is his own partial deafness, caused by a childhood furnace accident. His father saved the craft hand but not the hearing. Since then Nesh has been desperate to prove he can still judge true metal, still belong to the family line, still hear what matters. His relationship pressure comes from **Sella**, his closest friend and forbidden lover, a court listener who can identify guilt by resonance. Sella has been assigned to certify his mother’s bell. If she lies for him, she loses her ears by law. If she tells the truth, Nesh loses his mother to the furnace.
>
> The first irreversible pressure strikes when Nesh sneaks into the bell crypt to test the charge against his mother and discovers a bell with his own name already cast on the inside. It is old. Older than he is. When he touches it, every bell in Harrow Spire falls silent except the one in his chest. The city has been living under a false sound for twenty years, and someone engineered Nesh as the missing clapper. His mother is not the beginning of the scandal; she is the last witness. The vertical slice starts with him forced to choose whether to ring himself publicly and shatter civic law, or keep silent long enough to break his mother out before the furnace doors close.
>
> ---
>
> ## The Worm-Road Heir
>
> Across the red flats of **Keth Marrow**, cities travel inside colossal armored worms bred to chew through mineral deserts. Their ribs are streets, their stomachs are markets, their nerves are pilgrimage roads. **Rauk Senn**, a disgraced gut-navigator, wakes ankle-deep in digestive rain while his city-worm convulses around him. His estranged daughter has cut open the sacred nerve map and stolen the route to the only oasis that can save them.
>
> Rauk wants the route back before the worm starves. Not because he loves the city council, not because he believes in the old laws, but because fifty thousand people live inside this animal: cooks hanging pots from cartilage beams, children sleeping in rib hammocks, surgeons patching ulcers in the avenue walls, miners scraping salt from the worm’s teeth. The strange condition is constant and physical. Architecture sweats. Weather is peristalsis. Doors are sphincters with brass handles. The poor live near acid pools and cough up bile mist. The rich occupy the skull and call themselves “forward-facing.”
>
> The local doctrine of the navigators is brutal: **never love anyone more than the route**. A navigator must be willing to sacrifice family, memory, and limb to keep the worm moving. Rauk once obeyed. Years ago, he sealed a flooded gut-section to save the city’s direction, trapping his wife and dozens of others behind a muscle gate. His daughter **Vey** survived because he dragged her out first; she has hated him for saving her in the same motion that killed her mother. Now Vey has joined the **Stillborn Compass**, a rebel band who believe the worm-cities should be stopped, opened, and forced to become settlements before they consume the last living desert.
>
> Active opposition comes from three sides at once: the city’s skull-council wants Rauk to retrieve the map and execute Vey quietly; the rebels want to expose that the oasis route leads through a breeding ground of smaller worms the city intends to slaughter; and the worm itself has begun rejecting Rauk, tightening passages around him as if remembering his old betrayal. His closest ally is **Omm**, a stomach-doctor who once loved Rauk’s wife and now treats him with precise, useful contempt. Omm can keep Rauk alive inside the convulsing body, but will not let him lie to himself about the cost of “saving everyone.”
>
> The first irreversible trouble comes when Rauk catches Vey in the nerve chapel and she shows him the stolen route tattooed under her own skin in living ink. It cannot be copied without flaying her, and she did that deliberately. Then the worm speaks for the first time in recorded history—not in words, but by rearranging its inner muscles into a path that leads away from the oasis. The city’s doctrine says worms are beasts, routes are math, and navigators are will. Rauk now has proof that the road may be alive, afraid, and begging not to be driven where humans want to go. His first playable choice is a knife-edge: protect Vey and doom the city’s timetable, betray her and keep the worm moving, or follow the animal’s impossible new route into territory no map admits exists.
>

More likely **Codex/model-side behavior**, not Honcho.

Honcho should not be involved here: this is seed workshop material under `data/seed-runs/.../agent/workshop`, before witnessed narrator canon is committed. Honcho memory is supposed to receive only rolled-out story canon, not planning artifacts.

But I also don’t see proof of persistent Codex session memory in our client: the Codex OAuth client sets `store=false`, uses a random `session_id`, and does not send `previous_response_id`. So I’d phrase the current root cause as:

1. **Not Honcho memory.**
2. **Not a tracked static fixture.**
3. **Probably model rut / account-side or provider-side familiarity, amplified by broad prompts.**
4. **Definitely a runtime acceptance bug:** Writer can ask Scenarist, read the answer, then output unrelated “fresh” germs and we accept it.

So the fix should not depend on proving hidden memory. We should enforce provenance: if Writer calls `ask_scenarist` during a workshop turn, the workshop output must either clearly use/compare that returned material or explicitly say it is discarding it and why. Otherwise hard fail that workshop turn and retry with the same context.

I ran 7 live Codex writer probes with fresh one-shot calls, then removed the temporary probe command. Repo is clean afterward, and targeted tests pass: `go test -count=1 ./internal/codexoauth ./internal/prompt ./internal/seed`.

**What the probes showed**

1. **Direct memory probe:** Codex denied remembering prior Sans-Nom runs, including `Salt-Mirror Bride`, `Nacre-Hook`, `Bell-Maker’s Son`, `Harrow Spire`, `Nesh Ardent`, `Cult`, and `Bell`. That self-report is not proof, but it did not claim memory.

2. **Open seed prompt:** with a normal “operatic science-fantasy seed germs” prompt, it immediately generated familiar motif families: orchard, walking cathedral, bells, saltwater memory, vows-as-law, family obligation.

3. **Blank-project prompt:** even when told “use only this prompt,” it still generated orchard, sect/monks, cathedral, living body-city, civic council, memory/dream machinery.

4. **Scenarist-grounded prompt:** when explicitly forced to use only the four Scenarist sparks, it behaved well. It stayed on `Debt-Skin`, `Speaking Tomb`, `Hunger Contract`, `Refusal Rite`, and even said it felt tempted to introduce bells/mirrors/salt/worms but avoided them because of the grounding rule.

5. **Why choose one:** given only the four Scenarist sparks, it chose `Refusal Rite` because “first playable vertical slice” strongly pulls it toward a ritual refusal scene with a clear player verb.

6. **Motif audit prompt:** when asked to generate 3 germs and then count motif families, it used **all six** listed families: bell/sound, cult/rite, debt, witness/testimony, drowned/salt/mirror, living city/animal architecture.

**Conclusion**

This does **not** look like Honcho memory. It also does not look like an explicit Codex previous-response chain: the client uses `store=false`, random `session_id`, and no `previous_response_id`.

The stronger explanation is: the current creative prompt vocabulary creates a very strong attractor basin. Words like `operatic`, `science-fantasy comics`, `local doctrine`, `body pressure`, `witness memory`, `relationship wounds`, and `first irreversible pressure` naturally collapse into bells, rites, debts, testimony, salt/mirrors, living cities, family sacrifice.

The real runtime bug is that we accept Writer output even when it ignores the Scenarist artifact it just requested. The next fix should be structural: after `ask_scenarist`, require the Writer workshop output to either use/compare the returned Scenarist material or explicitly discard it with reasons. Otherwise fail that workshop turn and retry with the same context.

> hummm, feel like theres also a prompt issue, the motif may be to descriptive

Yes. I think the motif list is too *semantically loaded*. We keep giving the Writer a palette like:

`body / taboo / witness memory / social doctrine / operatic SF / philosophical violence / material condition / irreversible pressure`

That reads less like taste guidance and more like a shopping list. The model then dutifully assembles “bells + rites + debt + testimony + living architecture” because those are the most available symbols for that palette.

I’d change the prompt shape like this:

- Remove most motif nouns from default Writer prompts: especially `witness memory`, `body law`, `taboo`, `doctrine`, `philosophical violence`, maybe even `operatic`.
- Replace with process/taste guidance:
  - “Start with a person who wants something specific today.”
  - “Put someone emotionally credible in the way.”
  - “Let the world’s strangeness appear through work, tools, danger, habits, or relationships.”
  - “Prefer one concrete pressure over a full invented social system.”
- Stop requiring each germ to include `strange material condition`. That phrase basically summons world-mechanics soup.
- Make “local rule/doctrine” optional in workshop turns. It belongs in the later bundle/bible, not in every first idea.
- Use Scenarist for the flavorful motif push only after a grounded human situation exists.

A better imagination prompt would be closer to:

> Invent 3 story starts. Each begins with one person trying to do one urgent thing before someone else stops them. Give the place, the relationship wound, the immediate obstacle, and the first choice. Let any science-fantasy strangeness emerge from the job, setting, or danger. Keep the premise playable before it becomes mythic.

That should produce less “civic metaphysics factory” and more actual story engines.

**gpt-5.4/high Results**

| Probe | Prompt style | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 01 minimal | “3 playable science-fantasy starts” | Already produced `The Bell Beneath the Ice`, temple, priest, heresy, God Engine. Motif counts: `cult/rite=5`, `bell/sound=4`. |
| 02 human-first | person, urgent want, opposing person, wound, place | Better, but still saint/cathedral/memory quarry. Counts: `living-body=5`, `witness=5`, `salt/mirror/drowned=4`. |
| 03 light taste | emotionally specific, lived-in, avoid whole system | Still gothic: shrine-bells, debt payments, priests, memory plates, archive bells. Counts: `bell/sound=3`, `salt/mirror/drowned=3`, `witness=3`. |
| 04 source DNA lite | family pressure, body/tech stress, refusal, material consequence | Cleaner and more action-oriented. Still has cathedral-sized storm barge / living beast / dowry. Counts: `living-body=9`, `debt=3`, `salt/mirror/drowned=3`. |
| 05 current descriptive | vivid image, wound, relationship pressure, strange material, witness memory, binding doctrine | Motif explosion. Counts: `witness=15`, `living-body=10`, `law/doctrine=6`. |
| 06 heavy motif palette | body law, taboo, witness-bound memory, social enforcement, doctrine, etc. | Total soup. Counts: `witness=33`, `law/doctrine=24`, `debt=7`, `living-body=7`. |
| 07 grounded sparks | use only 3 mundane Scenarist sparks | Much cleaner. Counts: `debt=3`, `witness=2`, `bell/sound=1`. |

**Read**

Your cache hunch is possible, but this run points more strongly at **prompt attractor vocabulary** than model version. `gpt-5.4/high` behaves like `gpt-5.5/high`: once the prompt says `science-fantasy`, `operatic`, `witness`, `doctrine`, `body law`, `taboo`, or even just leaves “comic science-fantasy” wide open, the model reaches for bells/cathedrals/saints/rites/debts/memory-law.

The cleanest result was the grounded-transform prompt: start with plain human/action sparks, then add only one strange element that grows from the job/place. That suggests the seed pipeline should generate mundane dramatic engines first, then weird them up second.

> *   **Relationship Pressure:** The player’s sibling, a decorated Guard, is the one tasked with protecting the shipment and will be forced to execute the player if any deception is detected during the audit.
> *   **Strange Material Condition:** *The Hunger-Mist*—a seasonal atmospheric phenomenon that causes rapid, predatory cellular mutation in anything not encased in sanctified lead-glass.
> *   **First Irreversible Pressure:** The shipment has been breached by scavengers; to prevent the "Sacred Specimen" from escaping and triggering a planetary-scale retaliation, the player must use an experimental, flesh-binding resin that will permanently fuse their hand to the crate's handle.
> ```

Yeah, this is strong evidence. Gemma has no Codex memory and still falls into the same family of outputs: body-as-record, legal ownership, sect/corporate enforcers, irreversible bodily sacrifice, archive/tithe/vessel language.

So I’d call the main culprit the **shape of the prompt**, not provider memory.

The prompt is probably over-specifying the *ontology* of the story:

- `vivid image`
- `player desire`
- `active opposition`
- `character wound`
- `relationship pressure`
- `strange material condition`
- `first irreversible pressure`

That checklist basically asks the model to produce a dark science-fantasy RPG dossier. “Strange material condition” especially seems poisonous: models read it as “invent a body-system.” Then “wound” + “irreversible pressure” turns into “permanently damage the protagonist’s body.” Result: scars, grafts, living hulls, tithes, legal flesh, sects.

What I’d change next:

1. Remove the internal craft labels from the imagination prompt.
   Don’t ask for “strange material condition,” “character wound,” “relationship pressure,” etc. Those are our evaluation criteria, not writer-facing creative inputs.

2. Ask for **opening situations**, not germs.
   “Germ” seems to invite premise taxonomy. “Opening situation” invites scene.

3. Force variety through ordinary story engines, not motif words:
   job, rescue, theft, repair, crossing, negotiation, performance, escape, trial, delivery, sabotage.

A better imagination prompt shape might be:

```text
Invent 3 possible opening situations for a playable science-fantasy story.

Write each as 3-5 short paragraphs, like the first page of a comic issue:
- a person is trying to do one urgent thing today;
- another specific person is making that harder;
- the place, tools, weather, work, danger, or social habit reveal the strange world;
- the ending presents the first player choice.

Make the three situations feel different from each other: different jobs, places, emotional relationships, and kinds of trouble. Depth over coverage.
```

Then after each situation:

```text
Add two short notes:
- Why it could be playable
- What risk the Writer should fix later
```

This keeps the creative target, but stops feeding the motif machine its favorite ingredients.

> alright,... thought time.
>
> I think we won't be able to get original story that are interesting out of llm,... or they wont be original.
> what you think

I think your instinct is partly right, but I’d phrase it more narrowly:

LLMs are bad at inventing *interesting originality from taste words*. If we ask for “operatic science-fantasy, taboo, doctrine, body pressure, consequence,” they synthesize the average of that cloud. It feels rich for 20 seconds, then you notice the same bells, saints, scars, laws, memory archives, living bodies. That is not really imagination. It is motif completion.

But I don’t think that means we can’t get interesting original stories out of the system. It means originality has to come from **process**, not from the model’s raw first idea.

The better shape is probably:

1. Generate grounded situations first
   Jobs, weather, logistics, money, family, tools, broken infrastructure, local politics. This gives the story friction that is not already genre-coded.

2. Add weirdness from material cause
   Not “a doctrine says X,” but “this town survives because pumps, algae tanks, heat cells, bad roads, labor contracts, etc.” Then the strange grows out of survival.

3. Use LLMs as dramatizers/editors, not sole inventors
   They are good at: pressure, consequence, scene options, emotional sharpening, continuity. They are weaker at: genuine first principles originality.

4. Make taste arrive late
   Metabarons/source DNA should probably be an *editorial lens after a concrete premise exists*, not a seed ingredient. “Make this feel bigger, harsher, more consequential” works better than “invent from this taste cloud.”

5. Kill most seeds
   A real creative process rejects a lot. We should expect 70-90% of generated seeds to be bland, derivative, or motify. The system needs taste gates and maybe human/admin picking.

So: if the goal is “press button, get great original story,” I’m skeptical.

If the goal is “build a workshop that produces rough material, stress-tests it, grounds it in concrete causes, and lets us curate/iterate,” I think it can work. The LLM is not the genius author. It’s the noisy writing room. The originality has to come from the constraints, the selection process, and the accumulated world state.

> what about if we rethinked the engine.
>
> that was actually my original idea..
>
> what if we made the gameplay faithful to the lorepack selected, the game **must** honored the lore in the story and choices.
>
> and every lore pack **must** define a short synopsis on the game story as the initial seed (a few rough story lines posing the bases)
>
> what you think?

I think this is a much better engine direction.

The current approach asks the LLM to invent an original mythic story from abstract taste. That is exactly where it collapses into motif soup. Your proposed approach gives the engine a **real gravitational center**: the lorepack is not vague influence, it is the playable world contract.

The key shift:

```text
Old:
Lorepack -> abstract DNA -> LLM invents original story

Better:
Lorepack -> authored playable premise -> LLM stages and branches lore-faithful play
```

That is a more honest use of LLMs. They are much better at **continuing, dramatizing, branching, and enforcing an existing story world** than inventing a fresh one from empty taste words.

I’d define each lorepack as something like:

```yaml
id: metabarons
mode: faithful_inspired # or canon, original_homage, public_domain, owned_ip
game_synopsis:
  title: "..."
  pitch: "..."
  opening_situation: "..."
  protagonist_role: "..."
  initial_pressure: "..."
  central_relationships:
    - "..."
  first_story_arc:
    - "..."
    - "..."
    - "..."
lore_contract:
  must_honor:
    - "Initiation has irreversible bodily/social cost."
    - "Family inheritance is pressure, not decoration."
    - "Violence has ritual, philosophical, and material consequence."
  allowed_surfaces:
    - "body-tech"
    - "dynastic pressure"
    - "witness narration"
  forbidden_moves:
    - "random resurrection roster"
    - "all-cast fanout"
    - "copying exact canon scenes unless mode=canon and rights allow it"
choice_contract:
  choices_should:
    - "force refusal, obedience, sacrifice, concealment, or betrayal"
    - "change social standing or bodily cost"
  choices_should_not:
    - "be generic navigation"
```

Then the Writer is no longer “invent me something original.” It becomes:

> Given this lorepack synopsis and lore contract, build the next playable packet that honors the pack.

That gives us much better taste gates too:

- Does this contradict lore?
- Does this choice feel like this lorepack?
- Does this branch preserve the core pressure?
- Is the story drifting into generic fantasy?
- Is the player being offered choices that the lore actually cares about?

One important caveat: if the game is ever public-facing, “faithful to lore” only works safely for lorepacks you own, licensed material, public-domain material, or packs written as original homages. For private prototyping, using Metabarons as a test corpus is fine creatively, but product-wise we should build the engine so lorepack `mode` is explicit.

My recommendation: yes, pivot toward this. Make lorepacks authored scenario packs, not just reference corpora. The LLM becomes a **lore-faithful scene and branch runner**, not the source of the story’s soul.

>
> # Lore-Faithful Engine Pivot Master Plan
>
> ## Summary
> Pivot Sans-Nom from “LLM invents an original story from lore influence” to “selected lorepack defines a playable story synopsis and lore contract; LLMs stage, branch, narrate, and verify lore-faithful play.” For v1 of this pivot, use **Faithful Canon Prototype** mode: fidelity beats originality, and the game must honor the selected lorepack’s story, constraints, and choice logic.
>
> Create the master planning document at `docs/project/lore-faithful-engine-master-plan.md`. That doc becomes the task source for the next implementation units and should link from `docs/project/decisions-log.md`.
>
> ## Phase Plan
> 1. **Master Plan Document**
>    - Write `docs/project/lore-faithful-engine-master-plan.md` with: current-state analysis, target engine model, lorepack scenario contract, phased implementation tasks, cleanup list, tests, and migration notes.
>    - Record the decision in `docs/project/decisions-log.md`: lorepacks become scenario contracts, not abstract influence sources.
>    - Include an explicit “next task units” checklist so future work can be picked up one phase at a time.
>
> 2. **Lorepack Scenario Contract**
>    - Extend lorepack metadata from reference-only fields into an authored gameplay contract.
>    - Required new concepts: `gameplay_mode`, short `game_synopsis`, `protagonist_role`, `opening_situation`, `initial_pressure`, `story_lines`, `must_honor`, `must_not_violate`, and `choice_principles`.
>    - Add validation so active lorepacks cannot seed a story without a synopsis and lore contract.
>    - Update the Metabarons pack as the first Faithful Canon Prototype pack.
>
> 3. **Seed Engine Pivot**
>    - Replace the current seed workshop premise-invention flow with “lorepack synopsis -> initial StoryBible + three-turn StoryPacket.”
>    - The seed Writer must not invent the premise. It packages the lorepack-authored synopsis into playable structure.
>    - The seed verifier becomes a lore-fidelity verifier: reject packets that contradict the pack, drift into generic fantasy, or offer choices that do not matter inside the lore contract.
>    - Keep the existing bounded `StoryPacket` and Narrator split.
>
> 4. **Runtime Lore Fidelity**
>    - Writer refresh and Narrator prompts should receive the active synopsis, current arc position, lore contract, and relevant retrieved lore.
>    - Choices should be evaluated against `choice_principles`: they must express the lorepack’s actual pressures, not generic navigation.
>    - Rename or reframe `LoreExpert` into a lore authority/reference role for fidelity checks. Scenarist remains optional for staging/scene criticism, not premise invention.
>    - Backstage/admin should surface lore-fidelity checks as first-class model/tool events.
>
> 5. **Cleanup And Simplification**
>    - Remove or retire seed workshop turns whose purpose is broad premise generation.
>    - Remove “DNA summary” prompt language where it substitutes for explicit scenario contracts.
>    - Remove anti-copy/originality boundaries from Faithful Canon Prototype paths; keep them only if a future pack declares homage/original mode.
>    - Keep `cmd/prompt-eval` as a dev diagnostic tool, but mark old germ/checklist probes as legacy attractor tests.
>    - Delete or rewrite tests that assert “no raw lore injection” when the new path intentionally injects curated pack synopsis/contract.
>
> ## Public Interfaces And Data Shape
> - `lore/packs/<pack_id>/lore-pack.json` becomes the source of both retrieval metadata and authored gameplay contract.
> - Story state should persist the selected `ground_lore_pack_id`, plus the selected scenario/mode if more than one scenario is later supported.
> - Seed generation input becomes pack-authored story material, not free-form workshop artifacts.
> - Existing story workspaces remain readable as legacy stories; no migration is required for old runs.
>
> ## Test Plan
> - Lorepack tests: active packs fail validation without synopsis, mode, must-honor rules, and choice principles.
> - Seed tests: generated seed prompt includes the pack synopsis/contract and does not ask for original premise invention.
> - Verifier tests: reject contradiction of pack contract, generic choices, missing lore pressure, or unsupported branch logic.
> - Runtime tests: Writer refresh and Narrator receive lore contract context; existing `StoryPacket` and scene-scoped Honcho behavior still work.
> - Regression: legacy stories still resume; `go test ./...` passes; static backend stays deterministic.
>
> ## Assumptions
> - Chosen mode for this pivot: **Faithful Canon Prototype**.
> - Master planning doc path: `docs/project/lore-faithful-engine-master-plan.md`.
> - The current Writer/Narrator split, bounded packets, agentfs, backstage view, and scene-scoped Honcho memory remain valuable and should be preserved.
> - The cleanup is part of the pivot: broad LLM story invention becomes legacy machinery, not the main seed path.
</details>

Current state in short: the repo already has lore packs as selectable content (`lore/packs/<id>/lore-pack.json`) and story state stores `ground_lore_pack_id`, but the seed engine still treats the pack as influence/DNA while the Writer invents an original seed through workshop turns. The pivot would promote lore packs from “reference/influence” to “scenario contract + story synopsis + lore rules,” then simplify or delete the invention-heavy workshop machinery.

I’m cloning a shallow copy into `/tmp` to inspect SDK boundaries and whether there is a Go-usable API, because the README alone is too brochure-shaped for an integration call.
>
> <details><summary>Searched web 2 times</summary>
>

>
> - Searched web for `https://github.com/tursodatabase/agentfs/blob/main/sdk/go/README.md`
> - Searched web for `https://github.com/tursodatabase/agentfs/blob/main/MANUAL.md`
>
> </details>
>
> </details>
</details>

Yes, we *can* use it, but I would not replace our current `internal/agentfs` with it right now.

What I found:
- `tursodatabase/agentfs` is a SQLite-backed virtual filesystem with FS, KV, and tool-call audit storage. It has a Go SDK: `github.com/tursodatabase/agentfs/sdk/go`.
- It also has a CLI with mount/exec support: Linux via FUSE, macOS via NFS.
- It is explicitly marked beta in the repo.
- The Go module resolves today as a pseudo-version, not a clean semver module tag, because the repo tags are root-level.

Fit against Sans-Nom:
- Our current [internal/agentfs](./internal/agentfs/agentfs.go:13) is not really a filesystem. It is a scoped OS workspace builder plus path guard.
- Our model tools currently need real OS paths: Codex `exec_command` runs shell commands inside `ToolRoot`, and Claude/Scenarist tools use `WorkDir` / `--add-dir`.
- Turso AgentFS via Go SDK gives a virtual DB filesystem, not directly a directory that shell/Claude can read. To expose it to existing tools, we would need the CLI mount/exec path, which adds NFS/FUSE runtime complexity.

My recommendation:
- Keep our current scoped workspace for now.
- Consider Turso AgentFS as a later audit/snapshot layer, not the immediate tool-root implementation.
- Best first experiment would be a mirror: after staging `story/`, `scenarists/`, and `lorepack/`, also write the same tree plus tool calls into `agent.db`. That gets queryability and replay value without changing runtime behavior.
- Full replacement only makes sense if we move away from shell/Claude file tools toward custom `read_file`, `readdir`, `grep` tools backed by the SDK.

Good candidate use later:
1. Per-run `agent.db` under `data/.../agent.db`.
2. Store staged files in AgentFS DB.
3. Record model/tool calls into its tool-call table.
4. Keep the OS workspace as compatibility bridge.
5. Later test mounted AgentFS for Claude providers.

Sources checked: [AgentFS repo](https://github.com/tursodatabase/agentfs), [Go SDK README](https://github.com/tursodatabase/agentfs/blob/main/sdk/go/README.md), [manual](https://github.com/tursodatabase/agentfs/blob/main/MANUAL.md), [spec](https://github.com/tursodatabase/agentfs/blob/main/SPEC.md).

No repo changes made. Working tree is clean.

> Grep result for rg -n "succession|honor|wound|ritual|warrior|dynasty" lorepack/wiki/lore.md
>
> command pipeline is too long
>
> whats the issue there?

<details><summary>1 previous message</summary>

> I’ll trace the local read-tool guard, because that error sounds like our wrapper rejected the command before `rg` ran. The key question is whether the guard is mistaking a normal `rg` invocation for a shell pipeline.
</details>

It’s a bug in our local read-tool guard, not an `rg` problem.

In [internal/codexoauth/local_tools.go](./internal/codexoauth/local_tools.go:549), we detect shell pipelines with:

```go
segments := strings.Split(command, "|")
```

So this valid grep regex:

```sh
rg -n "succession|honor|wound|ritual|warrior|dynasty" lorepack/wiki/lore.md
```

gets misread as a 6-part shell pipeline, even though the `|` characters are inside quotes and mean regex alternation. Since the guard allows max 4 pipeline segments, it returns `command pipeline is too long`.

Quick workaround:

```sh
rg -n -e succession -e honor -e wound -e ritual -e warrior -e dynasty lorepack/wiki/lore.md
```

Proper fix: make the validator split only on unquoted `|`, or better, use a shell parser for this read-only command validation.

> I’m going to add `mvdan.cc/sh/v3/syntax`; it’s the standard Go shell parser people reach for when they’re tired of being haunted by quotes. Then I’ll validate the AST shape instead of splitting on characters.

Implemented and pushed `f2503fb`.

The read-tool validator now uses `mvdan.cc/sh/v3/syntax` to parse shell ASTs instead of splitting on `|`, so quoted regex alternation works:

```sh
rg -n "succession|honor|wound|ritual|warrior|dynasty" lorepack/wiki/lore.md
```

It still rejects real unsafe/unsupported shell forms: long pipelines, `&&`, redirects, command substitution, env assignments, non-allowlisted commands, and workspace escapes.

Fixed the crash path.

Root cause: Honcho live peer IDs only allow `^[a-zA-Z0-9_-]+$`, but the story generated `player:saren_iku_no`. The bridge already normalized peer IDs for scene commits, but not for peer cards, scene context, or representations. So card seeding hit Honcho with the raw colon ID and exploded.

I changed [bridge/src/bridge/honcho_ops.py](./bridge/src/bridge/honcho_ops.py) so raw story/agent IDs stay unchanged everywhere outside Honcho, but live Honcho calls use normalized IDs consistently:
- `player:saren_iku_no` -> `player-saren_iku_no`
- card get/set normalizes peer and target
- scene context normalizes `peer_target`
- representation normalizes observer and observed
- commits were already normalized

I also stopped the old running sidecar on port `8787`, because otherwise `go run` would reuse the stale Python process.

Verification:

- `go test ./...` -> passed

Found the loop. It was not just prose taste.

Three things were causing it:

- The Writer context was truncating while dumping the full packet JSON, so recent canon and planning constraints could disappear before the model saw them.
- Writer refresh had no durable phase plan, so it kept escalating the same witness/proof/challenge moment.
- Story index refresh used upsert without replacement, so stale old packet docs stayed in Qdrant and resurfaced as “lore” hits, pulling the Writer back into earlier packets.

I patched it:

- [internal/contextbundle/render.go](./internal/contextbundle/render.go:64) now puts selected node, recent canon, and a story progression contract before the full packet reference.
- [internal/story/types.go](./internal/story/types.go:30) adds required `story_arc` support for new seed bibles.
- [internal/prompt/templates.go](./internal/prompt/templates.go:12) tells seed/refresh/verifier prompts not to spend the story peak in the runway or replay the same proof.
- [cmd/cli/main.go](./cmd/cli/main.go:3264) now replaces the remote story index on refresh, clearing stale packet docs.
- I also repaired the active ignored runtime bible at [bible.json](./data/stories/story-20260520-131909/bible.json) with a concrete `story_arc`.

Verification passed:

- `go test ./internal/contextbundle ./internal/prompt ./internal/seed ./internal/story ./internal/storyapp`
- `go test ./cmd/cli`
- `go test ./...`
- `git diff --check`

Resume from the current story and pick a `turn_8` choice. After the selected branch is committed, the next Writer refresh should be forced out of the repeated proof loop into challenge/memory/custody consequences.

Verified first: this was the hard 15-minute model-agent cap, not evidence of a hung local process.

The seed Writer request started at `2026-05-22T02:36:24Z` and failed at `2026-05-22T02:51:24Z`, exactly 15 minutes later. The run was active before that: Writer tool reads continued, LoreExpert ran and returned, and the Writer read the LoreExpert answer at `02:48:09Z`. So the timeout was too tight for the heavier lore-orientation seed path.

I changed the CLI model-agent timeout default from 15 minutes to 45 minutes and made it configurable:

```text
SANS_NOM_MODEL_TIMEOUT_MS
SANS_NOM_CODEX_TIMEOUT_MS
SANS_NOM_CLAUDE_TIMEOUT_MS
SANS_NOM_SCENARIST_TIMEOUT_MS
SANS_NOM_WRITER_AWAIT_TIMEOUT_MS
```

This now covers Codex runners, Claude runners, Scenarist provider calls, and Writer refresh await. I also documented it in [docs/README.md](./docs/README.md) and added tests for default/specific/env fallback behavior.

Yes, for the normal CLI-created LoreExpert tool.

Then [internal/loreexpert/tool.go](./internal/loreexpert/tool.go:174) calls `r.Runner.Run(ctx, promptText)`, so the model receives:

- system prompt: includes `LORE.md`
- user/task prompt: the LoreExpert question + retrieved snippets

Also, `MasterLorePath` is included in the LoreExpert cache key at [internal/loreexpert/tool.go](./internal/loreexpert/tool.go:407), so changing `LORE.md` invalidates cached answers.

Short take: Mirage is worth a spike, but I would not replace our `internal/agentfs` with it yet.

Mirage is a virtual filesystem plus shell executor for agents: mount data sources under one tree, then let agents use familiar commands like `cat`, `ls`, `grep`, `find`, pipes, redirects, etc. Its own docs say the shell is not `/bin/bash`; it uses a bash parser plus custom executor, so it only sees mounted resources rather than the host filesystem. That directly overlaps with the exact pain we just fixed: command validation, workspace scoping, and accidental leakage from repo/test/generated surfaces. Sources: [GitHub README](https://github.com/strukto-ai/mirage), [docs intro](https://docs.mirage.strukto.ai/), [docs index](https://docs.mirage.strukto.ai/llms.txt).

**Best fit for Sans-Nom**
Mirage could become our model-visible tool filesystem layer, not our story engine. The promising use is:

- Mount only current staged run material:
  - `/story`
  - `/lorepack`
  - `/scenarists`
  - `/workshop`
  - maybe `/cache/lore-expert`
- Let Writer/Narrator/Scenarist use Mirage `execute()` instead of our hand-rolled local read command parser.
- Use Mirage snapshots to freeze the exact model-visible workspace for failed runs and replay/eval later.
- Potentially expose image/page/lore resources as virtual files without copying huge trees into agent workspaces.

**Why not drop it in now**
The project is young: GitHub shows a first public release on May 6, 2026, and the packages are still alpha-ish (`mirage-ai 0.0.2a0`, `@struktoai/mirage-core 0.0.2-alpha.0`). It also wants Python >=3.12 or Node >=20, while our runtime is Go. Integrating it would mean adding a sidecar/daemon or embedding a TS/Python service path. That is doable, but not something I would put in the live play loop before the current lore-faithful engine stabilizes.

**Architectural comparison**
Our current `internal/agentfs` is a staging and policy layer: it decides what files are copied into an agent workspace and blocks forbidden paths. Mirage is a richer VFS + command execution layer. It does not know Sans-Nom policy by itself, so we would still need our curated staging rules. But it could replace a chunk of fragile command parsing in `/Users/vincent/dev/sans-nom/internal/codexoauth/local_tools.go`.

Compared with Turso AgentFS: Turso AgentFS looked more like a durable audit/state substrate. Mirage is closer to the agent tool surface itself. For the problems we are currently hitting, Mirage is the more immediately relevant reference.

**Recommended spike**
I would add a small dev-only experiment, not live integration:

1. Create `cmd/mirage-eval` or `internal/agentfs/mirage_spike.md`.
2. Build a Mirage workspace from one seed run:
   - `/lorepack` from curated staged lorepack files only.
   - `/story` from active packet/state.
   - `/scenarists` from current run artifacts.
3. Run the same commands Writer tends to issue:
   - `cat lorepack/navigation.md`
   - `rg -n "succession|honor|wound" lorepack/wiki/lore.md lorepack/comics/volumes`
   - `find lorepack -maxdepth 4 -type f`
4. Verify forbidden surfaces are impossible:
   - no `peer-cards/runs`
   - no `provenance`
   - no `testdata`
   - no repo root
5. Compare logs with our current backstage tool logs.

Verdict: use Mirage as a serious design reference and spike candidate for `agentfs v2`. Do not adopt as a dependency in the live path until we prove it can run locally, snapshot deterministically, and preserve all Sans-Nom scoping rules.

Fixed.

The root issue was nastier than just retry budget: the structured `SeedBundle` schema defined `bible.metadata` as an object with **no allowed keys**, while the prompt and verifier required resume metadata. So the Writer was being pushed toward `{}` and then the Nerd Verifier rejected it. Tiny trapdoor.

Changed:

- `/Users/vincent/dev/sans-nom/internal/prompt/codex.go`
  - `bible.metadata` now requires concrete string fields:
    `seed_version`, `generated_at`, `resume_point`, `current_checkpoint`, `continuation_hooks`, `canon_validated`, `open_threads`, `gameplay_mode`, `ground_lore_pack_id`.

- `/Users/vincent/dev/sans-nom/internal/story/types.go`
  - local validation now rejects missing/empty resume metadata before the verifier.

- `/Users/vincent/dev/sans-nom/internal/seed/seed.go`
  - repair feedback explicitly tells the Writer how to fix metadata.
  - static default bundle now has valid metadata.

- `/Users/vincent/dev/sans-nom/cmd/cli/main.go`
  - live seed generation now uses `MaxIterations: 3`, so it is still bounded: initial attempt plus two repair passes, no indefinite retry loop.

Added regression coverage for empty metadata retry and schema metadata fields.

>       "description": "A human-born Metabunker witness-keeper with a metal throat-grill, keyed hands, and servant access to the Hall of Weapons. They are not noble, not a judge, and not free; their body is part of the initiation machinery they maintain.",

>       "boundary": "Iri-Ka will not call an unwitnessed lie clean, but they may still choose whose body has to pay for an incomplete truth."
